questions.question: According to ICH recommendations, what is the minimum number of determinations needed to assess the accuracy of an analytical procedure?

options.A: Three determinations, repeated three times at a single concentration (100% of the test concentration)
options.B: Nine determinations covering at least three concentrations, with three replicates at each concentration
options.C: Six determinations, repeated six times at 100% of the test concentration, without covering the whole range
options.D: Twelve determinations covering four concentrations, with three replicates at each concentration

questions.explanation: ICH recommends that accuracy be assessed using a minimum of nine determinations over a minimum of three concentration levels covering the specified range (three replicates at each level). "Six determinations at 100% of the test concentration" is an alternative approach for repeatability, not a requirement for accuracy.

questions.question: Within the same laboratory, the same procedure is run on different days by different analysts using different equipment. Which type of precision is being evaluated?

options.A: Repeatability, because the entire test is performed in the same laboratory
options.B: Reproducibility, because different people and different equipment are involved
options.C: Accuracy, because the variability comes from the analysts and equipment

questions.explanation: Repeatability is the same analyst, the same equipment, over a short period of time. Intermediate precision (also called ruggedness) is the variability within a laboratory caused by different days, analysts, or equipment. Reproducibility is between laboratories, for example in collaborative studies.

questions.question: For instrumental procedures that exhibit baseline noise, which statement about generally acceptable signal-to-noise ratios is correct?

options.A: Detection limit about 2:1 or 3:1; quantitation limit about 10:1
options.B: Detection limit about 10:1; quantitation limit about 2:1 or 3:1
options.C: Both the detection limit and the quantitation limit about 10:1
options.D: Detection limit about 20:1; quantitation limit about 100:1

questions.explanation: The detection limit is the lowest amount that can be detected but not necessarily quantitated, with a typically acceptable signal-to-noise ratio of 2:1 or 3:1. The quantitation limit is the lowest amount that can be determined with acceptable precision and accuracy, typically at 10:1, so it requires a stronger signal.

questions.question: According to Table 2, which analytical performance characteristic is required for Category IV (identification tests)?
questions.explanation: Category IV covers identification tests. In Table 2 only specificity is marked "Yes" and all other characteristics are "No", because the purpose of an identification test is to confirm the identity of the analyte. Category I requires accuracy, precision, specificity, linearity, and range, but not detection limit or quantitation limit.

questions.question: According to the ICH minimum requirements, what is the range for the assay of a drug substance or finished product, and what is the minimum number of concentrations for evaluating linearity?

options.A: 50% to 120% of the test concentration; at least three concentrations
options.B: 80% to 120% of the test concentration; at least five concentrations
options.C: 70% to 130% of the test concentration; at least nine concentrations
options.D: 90% to 110% of the test concentration; at least two concentrations

questions.explanation: ICH recommends at least five concentrations for linearity, and the minimum range for an assay is 80%-120% of the test concentration. "50% to 120%" is for the determination of impurities (50%-120% of the acceptance criterion), and "70% to 130%" is the minimum range for content uniformity.
